title: What is an RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset) — immutable, partitioned, lazily evaluated, fault-tolerant through lineage — and why is immutability important (thread-safety, deterministic recomputation, functional programming style)?
shortTitle: What is an RDD and why immutability matters

s1_definition.profdef: An RDD, or Resilient Distributed Dataset, is Spark's original core abstraction — an immutable, partitioned collection of records that is distributed across the executors of a cluster. It is lazily evaluated, meaning transformations only build a plan and nothing runs until an action is called, and it is fault-tolerant through lineage, meaning Spark records the sequence of transformations that produced it so that any lost partition can be recomputed rather than restored from a backup. Immutability is central: every transformation produces a new RDD instead of mutating the old one.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of an RDD as a stack of photocopied ledger pages spread across many clerks' desks at the National Bank of India. Nobody is allowed to scribble on a page; if you want a filtered version, you make a fresh copy with only the rows you want and leave the original untouched. Because nobody edits the originals, two clerks can read the same page at the same time without conflict, and if one clerk's desk catches fire, the manager just replays the exact steps that produced those pages to rebuild them. That read-only, replay-from-recipe discipline is what makes the whole system safe and recoverable.
s1_definition.oneliner: An RDD is an immutable, partitioned, lazily-evaluated, lineage-recoverable distributed collection, and its immutability is what makes parallelism safe and recomputation deterministic.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An RDD, or Resilient Distributed Dataset, is Spark's original core abstraction — an immutable, partitioned collection of records that is distributed across the executors of a cluster. It is lazily evaluated, meaning transformations only build a plan and nothing runs until an action is called, and it is fault-tolerant through lineage, meaning Spark records the sequence of transformations that produced it so that any lost partition can be recomputed rather than restored from a backup. Immutability is central: every transformation produces a new RDD instead of mutating the old one.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of an RDD as a stack of photocopied ledger pages spread across many clerks' desks at the National Bank of India. Nobody is allowed to scribble on a page; if you want a filtered version, you make a fresh copy with only the rows you want and leave the original untouched. Because nobody edits the originals, two clerks can read the same page at the same time without conflict, and if one clerk's desk catches fire, the manager just replays the exact steps that produced those pages to rebuild them. That read-only, replay-from-recipe discipline is what makes the whole system safe and recoverable.

**One line to remember:** An RDD is an immutable, partitioned, lazily-evaluated, lineage-recoverable distributed collection, and its immutability is what makes parallelism safe and recomputation deterministic.

sections.s2_technical:
An RDD has four defining qualities. It is resilient because it can rebuild lost data from lineage. It is distributed because its records are split into partitions that live across the executors. It is a dataset because it is a collection of records of some type. And although the newer DataFrame and Dataset APIs are what you use day to day, they are built on top of RDDs, so understanding the RDD explains how everything underneath behaves.

Immutability means that once an RDD is created, it cannot be changed. Every transformation like filter or map returns a brand-new RDD that describes how to derive itself from its parent, leaving the parent intact. This matters for three concrete reasons. First, thread-safety: because partitions are read-only, many tasks can process them in parallel across cores and machines without locks or race conditions, which is essential when hundreds of tasks run at once. Second, deterministic recomputation: if a partition is lost, Spark re-applies the exact same transformations to the exact same parent data and gets the exact same result, which is only safe because nothing mutates along the way. Third, a clean functional style: transformations are pure functions that take an input RDD and produce an output RDD, which makes the computation easy to reason about and to optimize.

Lazy evaluation works hand in hand with immutability. When you chain filter then map then groupBy, Spark does not run anything; it just builds a lineage graph of these transformations. Only when you call an action — count, collect, saveAsTextFile — does Spark look at the whole chain, optimize it, and execute it. This lets Spark fuse operations and avoid materializing intermediate results it does not need.

Fault tolerance through lineage is the resilient part. Spark stores the directed acyclic graph of transformations that built each RDD. If an executor dies and takes a cached partition with it, Spark does not fail the job; it finds the lineage for that one partition and recomputes only it from its parent, not the entire dataset. A senior nuance is that very long lineage chains can make recomputation expensive, which is exactly why checkpointing exists — it writes an RDD to reliable storage and truncates the lineage so recovery does not have to replay hundreds of steps. In a bank, this is the difference between a failed node causing a small recompute versus restarting an eight-hour job from scratch.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Many clerks must read the same ledger data in parallel without corrupting each other's work. This is exactly why an RDD is immutable and therefore thread-safe.

Problem 2 — When a desk fails, the bank cannot afford to redo the entire day's work. This is exactly fault tolerance through lineage — replay only the lost partition's recipe.

Problem 3 — The bank wants to describe a chain of cleaning and filtering steps without running them one expensive step at a time. This is exactly lazy evaluation building a lineage graph.

The mini-project models a tiny RDD in Java. `SimpleRdd` holds partitions and a reference to its parent plus the function that produced it (its lineage). `filter` and `map` return new `SimpleRdd` objects without mutating the parent. Calling the action `collect` triggers evaluation. A `recomputePartition` method simulates recovering a lost partition by replaying the lineage from the parent. The demo filters Rajesh's and Priya's transactions, maps amounts, collects, and then recomputes a "lost" partition to prove lineage recovery.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the RDD concept demo
java -cp target/rdd-concept-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.rdd.RddDemo

# Reference: equivalent real Spark (Scala) operations
#   val base = sc.parallelize(txns, 8)          // immutable, 8 partitions
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four transactions in two partitions — partition 0 has Rajesh Rs.1000 and Priya Rs.500, partition 1 has Rajesh Rs.3000 and Priya Rs.200.

Step 1: The base RDD is created holding the two partitions. The data is physically present and immutable; any read makes a defensive copy.

Step 2: Calling filter builds a new RDD that records "keep only SAV2001" as lineage. No data is touched and nothing runs. The base RDD is unchanged.

Step 3: Calling map builds another new RDD recording "extract amount." Again lazy — we now have a three-level lineage chain: base, then filtered, then mapped.

Step 4: Calling collect is an action, so evaluation starts. For each partition, Spark replays the lineage: it reads the base partition, applies the filter, then applies the map.

Step 5: Partition 0 yields Rs.1000 (Priya's Rs.500 was filtered out) and partition 1 yields Rs.3000. The collected result is the list containing Rs.1000 and Rs.3000.

Step 6: We simulate losing partition 1. Because the lineage is recorded and every step is a pure function on immutable data, recomputePartition replays base-filter-map for partition 1 only and deterministically rebuilds Rs.3000 — no backup needed.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] ACTION collect() triggers execution of the lineage
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] Rajesh amounts = [1000, 3000]
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] partition 1 lost — recomputing from lineage
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] Recovered partition 1 = [3000]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Base RDD (immutable, 2 partitions)
  P0: [Rajesh 1000, Priya 500]      P1: [Rajesh 3000, Priya 200]
    │                                  │
    ▼  filter(acct==SAV2001)  (LAZY)   ▼
  Filtered RDD (new object, parent=Base, records recipe)
  P0: [Rajesh 1000]                  P1: [Rajesh 3000]
    │                                  │
    ▼  map(amount)  (LAZY)             ▼
  Mapped RDD (new object, parent=Filtered, records recipe)
    │                                  │
    └──────────────┬───────────────────┘
                   ▼  collect()  (ACTION — triggers execution)
            Result: [1000, 3000]

  ── Fault recovery ──
  P1 lost ──→ replay lineage(P1): Base.P1 → filter → map ──→ [3000]
             (deterministic because data is immutable + functions are pure)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Immutable RDD with Lineage ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Immutable Object: every transformation returns a NEW RDD    │
  │     WHY: thread-safety + deterministic recomputation         │
  │  Lazy/Deferred Execution: transformations record a recipe    │
  │     WHY: optimize the whole DAG before running               │
  │  Composite/Recursive: RDD holds parent → recursive compute   │
  │     WHY: replay lineage from base on partition loss          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: SimpleRdd only models a dataset + its lineage            │
  │  O: new transformation = new method, existing ones unchanged │
  │  L: filtered/mapped RDDs usable anywhere a SimpleRdd is      │
  │  D: transform stored as Function abstraction, not hardcoded  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             SimpleRdd<T>                 │
  │─────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ - basePartitions: List<List<T>>  (root) │
  │ - parent: SimpleRdd<Object>      ◆ owns  │ lineage link
  │ - transform: Function<...>               │
  │─────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ + filter(Predicate<T>): SimpleRdd<T>     │ lazy
  │ + map(Function<T,R>): SimpleRdd<R>       │ lazy
  │ + collect(): List<T>                     │ ACTION
  │ + computePartition(i): List<T>           │ replays lineage
  │ + recomputePartition(i): List<T>         │ fault recovery
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
        self-reference via parent (recursive lineage)

  ── State Diagram: RDD Partition ───────────────────────────────

  [DEFINED(lazy)] ──action──→ [COMPUTED] ──cache──→ [CACHED]
        ▲                                               │
        │                                   executor lost
        └───────── recompute from lineage ──────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. RddDemo.main()
  2.   → base.filter(...)     → new SimpleRdd (lineage only)
  3.   → .map(...)            → new SimpleRdd (lineage only)
  4.   → collect()            → ACTION
  5.     → computePartition(0)→ base→filter→map → [1000]
  6.     → computePartition(1)→ base→filter→map → [3000]
  7.   → recomputePartition(1)→ replays lineage → [3000]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An RDD, or Resilient Distributed Dataset, is Spark's original core abstraction: an immutable, partitioned collection of records distributed across the executors of a cluster. It has four properties worth stating precisely. It is distributed because its records are split into partitions that live across the cluster. It is lazily evaluated because transformations like filter and map only build a lineage graph and nothing actually runs until an action such as count or collect is called. It is fault-tolerant through lineage because Spark records the exact sequence of transformations that produced each partition. And it is immutable, which is the property everything else depends on.

Immutability matters for three concrete reasons. First, thread-safety: because partitions are read-only, hundreds of tasks can process them in parallel across cores and machines with no locks and no race conditions. Second, deterministic recomputation: when a partition is lost, Spark re-applies the identical transformations to the identical parent data and gets the identical result, which is only safe because nothing was mutated along the way. Third, a clean functional style: each transformation is a pure function from one RDD to a new RDD, which makes the computation easy to reason about and lets the optimizer fuse steps.

In my project at the National Bank of India I relied on this behaviour constantly, even though we mostly used DataFrames, which are built on RDDs. When an executor died during a long ledger-processing job, Spark did not fail the whole run; it used the lineage to recompute only the lost partitions from their parents, which was the difference between a small recompute and restarting an eight-hour job. The one caution I always mention is that very long lineage chains make recomputation expensive, so for deeply iterative work I used checkpointing to materialize an RDD to reliable storage and truncate the lineage, keeping recovery fast.
